procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 5th March, 1980 of the Punjab and Haryana High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 525 DBA of 1980.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Moga acquitted the appellant on March 14, 1980. The Punjab & Haryana High Court set aside the acquittal order in a judgment dated March 3, 1982, convicted the appellant under s. 7 read with s. 16 (i) (a) (i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for six months and a fine of Rs. 1000/-.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court by way of a Special Leave Petition challenging the judgment and sentence of the Punjab & Haryana High Court. The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment and sentence, and remanded the matter to the High Court for a fresh decision.

directions: The appeal is remanded to the High Court for a decision afresh with advertence to the observations made above.

issue.issue_text: Whether the word 'damaged' appearing in the proviso to sub-s. (2C) of s. 13 of the Act is susceptible of a wider construction as to include damage due to any cause including decomposition.

law: The central legal question is the interpretation of the word 'damaged' in the proviso to sub-section (2C) of section 13 of the Act.

The Court considered two opposing views: a narrow view where 'damaged' means only damage from an improperly sealed container, and a wider view where it includes damage from any cause, including decomposition.
application: The Supreme Court sided with the wider interpretation, stating that the word 'damaged' must be construed in furtherance of the object and purpose of the legislation.
The Court reasoned that a narrow construction would frustrate the intent of Parliament. It held that a sample could be damaged for various reasons, such as breakage, leakage, or decomposition.

However, the Court qualified this wider interpretation by defining the timeframe in which the damage must occur. It disagreed with the view that the damage must happen only after the sample has been dispatched or is in transit.

The Court clarified that for the proviso to apply, the damage (including decomposition) must take place *after* the court has directed that part of the sample to be sent to the Central Food Laboratory, but it is not necessary for the damage to occur during the actual transit.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the word 'damaged' must be given a wider construction to mean 'damaged due to any cause, including decomposition'. However, it specified that this damage must occur after the court directs the sample to be sent to the Central Food Laboratory, regardless of whether it happens before or during the actual transit. This qualifies the full adoption of the wider view, hence the 'partly' answer.

issue.issue_text: Whether the kutcha khoya sold by the appellant was 'adulterated' i.e. not of the nature, substance or quality prescribed by law.

facts: A sample of kutcha khoya was taken from the appellant's shop.
The initial analysis by the Public Analyst found the fat content to be 25%, which was above the minimum standard of 20%.
A subsequent analysis by the Director, Central Food Laboratory (CFL), Ghaziabad, found the fat content to be 33.12%.

Despite the fat content being well above the minimum, the Ghaziabad CFL report concluded the sample was adulterated, adding a note that 'the extracted fat content did not comply with the standards of milk fat for the State of Punjab'.
The prosecution was unable to produce any notification or evidence of a special, higher fat content standard for khoya in Punjab.
application: The Supreme Court found the conflicting evidence to be "rather disturbing".
It questioned the significant and unexplained discrepancy in the fat content reported by the two different labs (25% vs. 33.12%).
The Court was also unclear as to why the Ghaziabad CFL deemed the sample adulterated when its fat content was significantly higher than the prescribed minimum standard.
It noted that the reason for the adulteration finding was ambiguous—it could have been due to a foreign substance or a supposed higher standard for Punjab, but there was no evidence for the latter.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not definitively decide whether the khoya was adulterated. Due to the major inconsistencies and unanswered questions in the evidence, it concluded that the matter required further investigation. Therefore, the Court remitted the case back to the High Court for a fresh decision, with instructions to seek clarification from the Ghaziabad laboratory or take other steps to resolve the evidentiary conflicts.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the word 'damaged' appearing in the proviso to sub-s. (2C) of s. 13 of the Act is susceptible of a wider construction as to include damage due to any cause including decomposition.
appellant_arguments: The word 'damaged' should be interpreted narrowly and should not include natural decomposition. Therefore, the magistrate was not justified in sending the second part of the sample for analysis after the first was found to have decomposed.
respondent_arguments: The word 'damaged' should be given a wider construction to include damage from any cause, including decomposition, thus validating the magistrate's action of sending the remaining part of the sample for analysis.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the kutcha khoya sold by the appellant was 'adulterated' i.e. not of the nature, substance or quality prescribed by law.
appellant_arguments: The kutcha khoya sold was not adulterated within the meaning of s. 2(ia)(l) of the Act, and therefore, the conviction was improper.
respondent_arguments: The kutcha khoya was adulterated, as established by the evidence and testimony of expert witnesses (Dr. Paramjit Singh and Dr. Narinder Kumar), justifying the conviction.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In statutory interpretation, while the language employed is the primary determining factor, words used by the Legislature do not always bear a plain meaning and must take their color from the context in which they appear.
obiter: There is a conflict of opinion between the High Courts and also within the same High Court as to the construction of the word investigation.
It appears that the attention of the High Court was not drawn to the finding reached by the learned Magistrate based on the report of the Director, Central Food Laboratory, Ghaziabad.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The conviction cannot be sustained because the primary evidence, the certificate from the Central Food Laboratory, is internally contradictory. While the certificate is deemed 'final and conclusive evidence' and states the sample was 'adulterated', it also shows that the fat content was in excess of the prescribed minimum. This factual ambiguity within the report itself means it could not form the sole basis for conviction, necessitating a remand to the High Court for a fresh decision.
legal_tests_applied: Purposive interpretation of a statute: The court interpreted the word 'damaged' by looking at the legislative intent behind the requirement for multiple samples, stating, 'The whole purpose of depositing two parts of the sample with the Local (Health) Authority is that if one of the parts of the sample is lost or damaged for any reason whatever, the remaining part may still be available for analysis.'

Statutory finality of evidence: The court considered the rule under the proviso to sub-s. (5) of s. 13 of the Act, which makes the certificate of the Director, Central Food Laboratory, 'final and conclusive evidence of the facts stated therein.'
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument for a narrow interpretation of the word 'damaged' was rejected, as the court held that the term 'has to be given a wider meaning' to include decomposition, in order to fulfill the purpose of the Act.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument for a wider construction of the word 'damaged' was accepted by the court, which found that the legislative purpose of requiring multiple samples was to ensure one would be available for analysis even if another was 'lost or damaged for any reason whatever.'
policy_considerations: The court's interpretation is driven by the public policy of ensuring the food safety law functions effectively. The whole purpose of the multi-sample system is to prevent the process from being defeated if one sample becomes unusable, thus ensuring that an analysis can be completed.
